paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Salmon is one of the most popular fish among consumers and is regarded as being part of a healthy diet, since it is high in protein as well as omega-3 fatty acids and vitamin D. The growing demand for the fish has led to the rapid growth of the salmon farming industry, with the establishment of fish farms around the world, where the salmon are bred and raised to maturity. But a surge of parasitic sea-lice is now disrupting these salmon farms in major salmon-producing countries such as the US, Canada, Scotland, Norway and Chile. The tiny lice attach themselves to the salmon and eat their blood and skin, killing them or rendering them unsuitable for dinner tables. Fish farmers worldwide consider sea lice the biggest threat to their industry and say the persistent problem is making the fish more expensive to consumers. The lice are present in the wild, but thrive in the tightly packed ocean pens used for fish-farming, said Shawn Robinson, a scientist with the Canadian Department of Fisheries and Oceans. ‘There are not enough tools right now to allow the farmer to really effectively deal with it,’ he said.

The tiny lice attach themselves to the salmon and eat their blood and skin, killing them or rendering them unsuitable for dinner tables. The lice are present in the wild, but thrive in the tightly packed ocean pens used for fish-farming, said Shawn Robinson, a scientist with the Canadian Department of Fisheries and Oceans. ‘There are not enough tools right now to allow the farmer to really effectively deal with it,’ he said.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The lice are actually tiny crustaceans. They can grow to about the size of a pea and lay thousands of eggs in their brief lifetime. But Atlantic salmon have held their own with sea-lice in the wild for centuries, and fish farmers have managed them in aquaculture environments for many years. ‘It was not until 1994 that farmers in Canada identified the lice as a problem,’ said Jonathan Carr, executive director of research and environment with the Atlantic Salmon Federation. Feeding fish a pesticide with the active ingredient of emamectin benzoate became the tool of choice to control lice. Carr said: But around 2009 the lice appeared to become resistant to the pesticide, and since then this had happened before reacting. The industry's key mistake was waiting until after this game. Kris Nicholls, chief operating officer at Cooke Aquaculture Inc., says that as in Canada, who are a major player in world salmon farming, says that as the pesticide lost its effectiveness, there was increasing demand for new treatments.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Scientists and fish farmers are working on new ways to control the pests. But so far, it has been an uphill struggle. 'Our work has to be quicker than the evolution of the lice,' said Jake Elliott, vice-president of Cooke Aquaculture. The worldwide supply of salmon fell almost 10 percent last year, with Norway, the largest producer in the world, being especially hard hit. In Norway, there are hundreds of times more salmon in aquaculture than in the wild. And fish with lice attached to them can potentially escape their pens, carrying the lice into the open sea where they can affect wild fish. To stop this happening, Norwegian farmers are looking to use new closed-in pens that resemble giant cages instead of ones which are open at the top and allow the salmon to jump out.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: In an attempt to solve the problem of lice without using chemicals, farmers in North America and Europe are experimenting with using other species of fish such as wrasse to coexist with the salmon and eat the lice. 'We have about 100000 fish and the wrasse have cut our losses enormously. We haven' t had to use chemicals since August 2014. We find lice very occasionally but 99 percent of the time we are completely clean,' said Pete Robinson, a worker at the Wester Ross salmon company in Ullapool, Scotland. But even using wrasse is not a complete answer. Recent studies show that fish farms may be depleting wild wrasse numbers. To find an alternative solution, research into farming salmon along with some types of shellfish, which researchers have found will eat young sea lice, is also underway. At the other end of the technological spectrum, a Norwegian firm has developed a piece of equipment which can be lowered into a salmon pen, where it can identify individual lice on salmon swimming past, and zap them with a laser. The technology was developed in Norway and has successfully used there and in Scotland.

At the other end of the technological spectrum, a Norwegian firm has developed a piece of equipment which can be lowered into a salmon pen, where it can identify individual lice on salmon swimming past, and zap them with a laser. The technology was developed in Norway and has successfully used there and in Scotland.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Cooke Aquaculture is also working hard to solve the problem of lice. The company uses a pair of boats capable of pumping 10000 fish at a time into a hydrogen peroxide bath, which gets rid of most of the lice. However, it can also stress the fish, some of which may even die as a result. So, to avoid use of such chemicals the company has designed a $4-million vessel containing a series of tubes that propel 300 salmon a minute on a winding journey while washing them with warm water to remove lice. Cooke Aquaculture engineer Joel Halbe, who likened this to a 'waterslide park' for fish, said the cost to the salmon farming industry from sea lice is huge, and the fish-farming industry has no choice but to try such innovations.

groups.title: Dealing with sea lice on fish farms
content: In 1994, when sea lice first became a problem on fish farms, they were successfully treated with a {{24}} pesticide containing emamectin benzoate, but the lice later developed resistance to this. In Norway, farmers are planning to use special pens to prevent the spread of the lice to wild salmon.

In addition to, new methods of destroying the lice are being used, including the use of wrasse, which feed on the lice. Research is also being carried out on the use of {{25}} shellfish, as these can perform the same function as wrasse. In Norway, a way of killing the lice with a {{26}} laser has been invented.
